Escher Ceva Menelaus

GeometryTrianglesAlgebra
Game: Move the dots on a triangle and see whether its three cross-lines meet at one point.
How to play: Drag a dot with a mouse or finger, or focus it and use the arrow keys. Change the number boxes to split each side into more or fewer equal parts.
Look for the math

Two old triangle facts, Ceva's theorem and Menelaus' theorem, turn out to be two special cases of one equation. This applet lets you move six side dots and watch that equation decide whether three lines meet.

Turn side dots into numbers

On the side A2A3, the article measures B1 and C1 from opposite ends. If the side is split into N equal parts and a B dot is i ticks from its first corner, its number is b = (N−i)/i. A C dot i ticks from that same corner gives c = i/(N−i). A C dot at the corner itself gives c = 0. These are the same signed ratios used in barycentric coordinates: B1 has coordinates (0:b1:1) and C1 has (0:1:c1), with the other sides following the same pattern. The opening picture has b = (1/4, 3, 1/2) and c = (3/2, 0, 1/2).

One small quirk is kept from the Java applet: the number boxes read 3, 4, 5 on load, but the drawn grids are 3, 5, 4 until you move a box. Both are the same three side lengths, and the logic test pins the exact starting order.

One equation decides everything

The page states, and the logic test checks, that C1B2, C2B3 and C3B1 are concurrent exactly when

b1b2b3 + c1c2c3 + b1c1 + b2c2 + b3c3 = 1

The three line equations in barycentric coordinates have a coefficient determinant; it vanishes precisely when the left side is 1. The test compares that formula with the drawn lines at every integer dot choice on a 3-4-5 triangle (271 finite cases) and at 4,000 random choices with up to 30 parts per side. It also follows the applet's own Ratio() and Formula() methods a second time, from the bytecode, and a green dot appears here under the same |1 − F| < 0.01 test the applet uses.

Escher's twelve patterns

The page says that dividing the sides into 3, 4 and 5 parts gives twelve concurrences known to M. C. Escher. That claim is confirmed: put B one tick after C on every side, try all six ways of assigning 3, 4 and 5 to the three sides, and exactly two patterns per assignment work — twelve in all. The opening picture is one of them. Other integer dot choices can also satisfy the equation, so twelve counts Escher's adjacent-tick patterns, not every possible choice of six dots. This is a different Escher result from the Napoleon-hexagon applet called Escher's Theorem: that one uses 120° rotations and a tessellation, not triangle sides cut into 3, 4 and 5 pieces.

Ceva and Menelaus hide inside it

If each C dot sits at the first corner of its side, then c1 = c2 = c3 = 0 and the equation becomes b1b2b3 = 1, the Ceva condition. If each C dot is moved onto its B dot, then bici = 1, and the equation becomes b1b2b3 + 1/(b1b2b3) = −2, so the product is −1: Menelaus. The test confirms both reductions in 600 cases each.

Try putting every B dot one tick after its C dot, then change only one side: the green crossing disappears at once.
